chapter: Image, travel and Black, Brown and Beige
title: Clothes consciousness and the Aristocrats of Jazz
summary: Greer says Leo Bernstein paid for sharp clothes and the full dress suits set a trend.

story.theme_name: Brass bands, parades and jazz funerals
story.community_name: Parading for Mardi Gras and the clubs

blocks.x: So then when you all got the band together, it was like you and Ellington got guys to start being as conscious of --

Yeah, clothes conscious. And Leo Bernstein, the owner of the Kentucky Club, he wanted to see his bands dressed up. He'd say, "My band's the sharpest band in New York. And he keeps going down to the high priced and gets that -- all we had to tel him, "Man, I seen something down there that's too bad." He'd say, "Well, go get it, send the bill to
Now, do you think that has something to do with the trend of all the bands getting so sharp after you all?
It could be. I couldn't definitely say that.
Well, the reason I asked is because when I was studying ble) the old band book pictures --
The Jimmie Lunceford band, all dressed, all the bands started looking after their uniform and appearance, you know.

Yeah, because like I saw some old pictures of bands and before the Ellington band, from what I could tell by these books, I don't know, most of the guys had like pinstripe suits on, or maybe a tuxedo. But like all those things, I started noticing you all started wearing tuxedos with like these satin lapels.

Full dress suit. We had a black full dress suit, we had a white full dress suit. We had different combinations. I'm quite certain we were the first one that had that. That's why Lady Mountbatten nicknamed us 'The Aristocrats of Jazz'. We lived the part. We were the part. And everybody was very conscientious of their appearance, you know.
